query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor alloying addition that promotes the in situ formation of a lubricious, temperature‐responsive oxide phase will enhance the tribological performance of CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys across a wide temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without additional alloying elements.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a small concentration (e.g., on the order of a few atomic percent) of an element (for example, a refractory metal such as Re or another element known to form lubricious oxides) into the CoCrFeNi matrix to enable the development of a self-adaptive lubricious oxide during sliding.
generation.conditions: Tested under sliding conditions that span from room temperature up to 800 °C; variations in applied load and environmental partial pressures of oxygen are present to simulate operational changes.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a fine, stable oxide phase that precipitates in situ at the sliding interface and functions as a solid lubricant.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the modified alloy maintains a microstructure similar to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, while at elevated temperatures the introduced element oxidizes preferentially to form a continuous, lubricious oxide film, reducing friction and wear. The self-adaptive nature of the oxide film is expected to maintain low friction across a broad temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the modified alloy is predicted to exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rates at high temperatures (approaching 800 °C), and at least comparable, if not better, performance at lower temperatures due to the benign influence of the minor addition.
generation.baseline: Pure CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy exhibiting increasing coefficient of friction and wear rates as temperature rises.
generation.boundary: The improvement is anticipated to be effective under sliding wear conditions with moderate to high loads and in oxidizing environments; performance might be sensitive to extreme environmental conditions (e.g., very low/very high oxygen partial pressures) or loads beyond the tested range.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal concentration of the added element and the detailed kinetics of oxide formation across the temperature range are uncertain, as is the long-term stability of the lubricious film under cyclic or prolonged high-temperature operation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and one of the alloy modified with the minor addition. Subject both to sliding wear tests in an environment where oxygen partial pressure, load, and temperature are varied. Temperature should be ramped from room temperature to 800 °C, while loads are chosen to simulate relevant application conditions. Compare the evolution of the friction coefficient and wear rate as a function of temperature.
measurements: Coefficient of friction via real-time sensor measurements during sliding.
Wear rate quantified by weight loss and/or surface profilometry post-test.
Surface analysis through SEM/EDS or XRD to detect the formation of the lubricious oxide phase.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not exhibit a significantly lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate compared to the baseline across the full temperature range, or if the lubricious oxide phase is not detectable at high temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified.
